blocks.body:
Five students each list the projects they would accept. Can every student get a different acceptable project? If not, why not? The obvious obstruction is a group of, say, three students who between them accept only two projects. Hall's theorem (Philip Hall, 1935) says that this obstruction is the only one: if no group of students is short of projects, everyone can be served.

A second, harder question asks for a round trip through a graph that visits every vertex exactly once. Here no simple criterion is known or expected, but there are useful sufficient conditions, the most famous being Dirac's (1952): if every vertex is adjacent to at least half of the others, such a cycle exists. This lesson proves both theorems and states the Erdős–Gallai bound on graphs without long cycles.

blocks.title: Matching
blocks.body:
A matching in a graph is a set of edges no two of which share an end. A matching covers (or saturates) a vertex if the vertex is an end of one of its edges, and it is perfect if it covers every vertex.

A graph is bipartite with sides $X$ and $Y$ if $V = X \cup Y$ with $X \cap Y = \varnothing$ and every edge has one end in each side. For $S \subseteq X$, the neighbourhood $N(S)$ is the set of vertices in $Y$ adjacent to at least one vertex of $S$.

In the opening question, $X$ is the set of students, $Y$ the set of projects, and a matching covering $X$ is an assignment of distinct acceptable projects to all students.

blocks.title: Hall's marriage theorem
blocks.body:
A bipartite graph with sides $X$ and $Y$ has a matching covering $X$ if and only if
$$|N(S)| \ge |S| \quad \text{for every } S \subseteq X.$$

If a matching covers $X$, the vertices of $S$ are matched to $|S|$ distinct vertices, all in $N(S)$, so Hall's condition holds.

For the converse, induct on $|X|$. If $|X| = 0$ there is nothing to prove; if $|X| = 1$, Hall's condition gives the single vertex a neighbour. Suppose $|X| \ge 2$ and Hall's condition holds. There are two cases.

Case 1: $|N(S)| \ge |S| + 1$ for every non-empty $S \subsetneq X$. Pick any edge $xy$ with $x \in X$ (one exists, by the condition for $S = \{x\}$). Delete $x$ and $y$. In the remaining graph, a non-empty set $S \subseteq X \setminus \{x\}$ has lost at most the neighbour $y$, so it still has at least $|S| + 1 - 1 = |S|$ neighbours. By induction the remaining graph has a matching covering $X \setminus \{x\}$; add the edge $xy$.

Case 2: some non-empty $S_0 \subsetneq X$ has $|N(S_0)| = |S_0|$. Split the graph into two bipartite graphs: $G_1$ with sides $S_0$ and $N(S_0)$, and $G_2$ with sides $X \setminus S_0$ and $Y \setminus N(S_0)$, each keeping the edges of $G$ between its sides.

In $G_1$, every $S \subseteq S_0$ has all its $G$-neighbours inside $N(S_0)$, so its neighbourhood is the same as in $G$ and Hall's condition holds. In $G_2$, take $T \subseteq X \setminus S_0$ and let $N_2(T) = N(T) \setminus N(S_0)$ be its neighbourhood there. Then $N(T \cup S_0)$ is the disjoint union of $N(S_0)$ and $N_2(T)$, so
$$|N_2(T)| = |N(T \cup S_0)| - |N(S_0)| \ge |T| + |S_0| - |S_0| = |T|.$$
Both $G_1$ and $G_2$ have fewer than $|X|$ vertices on the $X$ side, so by induction they have matchings covering $S_0$ and $X \setminus S_0$. They use disjoint sets of $Y$-vertices, and together they cover $X$.

blocks.title: Consequences of Hall's theorem
blocks.body:
Hall's condition involves every subset, so it is not easier to check by brute force than searching for the matching. Its strength is in proofs: to show a matching exists you only need a counting argument for an arbitrary $S$.

The standard example is regular graphs. Suppose a bipartite graph is $k$-regular (every vertex has degree $k \ge 1$). Counting edges from each side gives $k|X| = k|Y|$, so $|X| = |Y|$. For $S \subseteq X$, the $k|S|$ edges leaving $S$ all end in $N(S)$, and the vertices of $N(S)$ have only $k|N(S)|$ edge-ends in total, so $k|S| \le k|N(S)|$. Hall's condition holds, and the matching covering $X$ is perfect. Removing it leaves a $(k-1)$-regular bipartite graph, so repeating the argument splits the edges into $k$ perfect matchings.

Hall's theorem is one of several equivalent min–max theorems. König's theorem (1931) says that in a bipartite graph the largest matching has the same size as the smallest set of vertices meeting every edge. The max-flow min-cut theorem for networks contains both. For graphs that are not bipartite, Tutte's theorem gives the corresponding criterion for a perfect matching.

blocks.title: Hamiltonian cycle
blocks.body:
A Hamiltonian cycle in a graph is a cycle that passes through every vertex exactly once. A graph with such a cycle is Hamiltonian. We write $\delta(G)$ for the minimum degree of $G$.

Compare Euler tours (see [[graph-basics]]), which use every edge once and have a simple criterion; deciding whether a Hamiltonian cycle exists is NP-complete.

blocks.title: Dirac's theorem
blocks.body:
Let $G$ be a graph on $n \ge 3$ vertices with $\delta(G) \ge n/2$. Then $G$ is Hamiltonian.

The hypothesis $n \ge 3$ is needed: the graph with two vertices and one edge has $\delta = 1 = n/2$, but no cycle at all.

First, $G$ is connected. If $u$ and $v$ are not adjacent, their neighbourhoods lie in the $n - 2$ other vertices and have sizes adding up to at least $n$, so they share a vertex, and $u, w, v$ is a path.

Let $P = v_0 v_1 \dots v_k$ be a longest path in $G$. Every neighbour of $v_0$ is on $P$, since otherwise $P$ could be extended at $v_0$; likewise for $v_k$. Since $v_0$ has at least $n/2 \ge 3/2$, hence at least $2$, neighbours, all on $P$, we have $k \ge 2$. Consider the index sets
$$A = \{\, i : 0 \le i \le k-1,\ v_0 v_{i+1} \in E \,\}, \qquad B = \{\, i : 0 \le i \le k-1,\ v_i v_k \in E \,\}.$$
Then $|A| = \deg v_0 \ge n/2$ and $|B| = \deg v_k \ge n/2$, and both lie in $\{0, 1, \dots, k-1\}$, which has $k \le n - 1$ elements. Since $|A| + |B| \ge n > k$, some index $i$ lies in both: $v_0 v_{i+1}$ and $v_i v_k$ are edges. Then
$$v_0\, v_{i+1}\, v_{i+2} \cdots v_k\, v_i\, v_{i-1} \cdots v_1\, v_0$$
is a cycle $C$ through all $k + 1$ vertices of $P$. (If $i = 0$ or $i = k-1$, the edge $v_0 v_k$ is present and $C$ is just $P$ closed up by it.)

If $C$ missed some vertex, then, $G$ being connected, some vertex $w$ outside $C$ would be adjacent to a vertex $v_j$ of $C$. Starting at $w$, stepping to $v_j$ and then going once around $C$ gives a path with $k + 2$ vertices, longer than $P$. That is impossible, so $C$ is a Hamiltonian cycle.

blocks.title: How sharp is Dirac's condition?
blocks.body:
The bound $n/2$ cannot be lowered. Take the complete bipartite graph $K_{m, m+1}$, with $n = 2m + 1$ vertices and minimum degree $m = (n-1)/2$. Any cycle in a bipartite graph alternates between the sides, so it contains equally many vertices from each side; a cycle through all $2m + 1$ vertices is therefore impossible.

On the other hand the condition is far from necessary: the cycle $C_n$ itself is Hamiltonian with minimum degree $2$. Ore (1960) proved a stronger sufficient condition by the same argument: if $\deg u + \deg v \ge n$ for every pair of non-adjacent vertices, with $n \ge 3$, then $G$ is Hamiltonian. The Petersen graph, which is $3$-regular on $10$ vertices, is a famous small graph that is not Hamiltonian; no degree condition of this type sees why.

blocks.title: Erdős–Gallai theorem (1959)
blocks.body:
Let $k \ge 3$. Every graph on $n$ vertices with more than $\frac{(k-1)(n-1)}{2}$ edges contains a cycle of length at least $k$.

Similarly, every graph on $n$ vertices with more than $\frac{(k-1)n}{2}$ edges contains a path with $k$ edges. We omit the proofs, which refine the longest-path argument above.

blocks.title: Why these bounds are the right ones
blocks.body:
Both bounds are attained. For the cycle version, glue copies of the complete graph $K_{k-1}$ together at one common vertex. If $n - 1$ is divisible by $k - 2$, this uses $(n-1)/(k-2)$ copies, each with $\binom{k-1}{2}$ edges, for a total of $\frac{(k-1)(n-1)}{2}$ edges. Every cycle stays inside one copy (the shared vertex is the only link between copies), so there is no cycle of length $k$ or more. For the path version, take disjoint copies of $K_k$: if $k \mid n$ this has $\frac{(k-1)n}{2}$ edges, and the longest path has $k - 1$ edges.

So among graphs on $n$ vertices, those with no long cycle have at most about $kn/2$ edges, which is linear in $n$. Contrast this with excluding a short cycle such as a triangle, where about $n^2/4$ edges are possible; this is the subject of [[extremal-graphs]].

blocks.title: Picking one card from each pile
blocks.body: A standard deck of $52$ cards ($13$ ranks, $4$ suits) is dealt into $13$ piles of $4$ cards each, in any way. Show that one can choose one card from each pile so that the $13$ chosen cards have $13$ different ranks.
blocks.solution:
Let $X$ be the set of piles and $Y$ the set of ranks, and join a pile to a rank if the pile contains at least one card of that rank. A matching covering $X$ is exactly a choice of different ranks, one present in each pile.

Check Hall's condition. Take any $s$ piles. They contain $4s$ cards. Each rank has only $4$ cards in the whole deck, so these $4s$ cards involve at least $s$ different ranks. So $|N(S)| \ge |S|$, and Hall's theorem gives the matching. (Since $|X| = |Y| = 13$ it is a perfect matching.)

blocks.title: Extending Latin rectangles
blocks.body: An $r \times n$ Latin rectangle is an $r \times n$ array filled with the numbers $1, \dots, n$ so that no number repeats in a row or in a column. Show that if $r < n$, every $r \times n$ Latin rectangle can be extended by a new row to an $(r+1) \times n$ Latin rectangle. Deduce that one can always complete it to an $n \times n$ Latin square.
blocks.solution:
Let $X$ be the set of columns and $Y = \{1, \dots, n\}$, and join column $c$ to number $j$ if $j$ does not yet appear in column $c$. A new row is exactly a perfect matching: each column gets a number missing from it, and different columns get different numbers.

Each column contains $r$ distinct numbers, so it is joined to $n - r$ numbers. Each number appears once in each of the $r$ rows, in $r$ different columns, so it is missing from exactly $n - r$ columns. The bipartite graph is $(n-r)$-regular with $n - r \ge 1$, and by the consequence of Hall's theorem above it has a perfect matching. Repeating the step $n - r$ times completes the array to a Latin square.

blocks.title: Pairing up acquaintances
blocks.body: In a group of $2m \ge 4$ people, each person knows at least $m$ of the others (knowing is mutual). Show that the people can be seated around a round table so that everyone knows both neighbours, and also that they can be split into $m$ pairs of acquaintances.
blocks.solution:
Make the people vertices and acquaintances edges. There are $n = 2m \ge 4 \ge 3$ vertices and each has degree at least $m = n/2$, so Dirac's theorem gives a Hamiltonian cycle $v_1 v_2 \dots v_{2m} v_1$. Seating people in that order around the table works.

The cycle has even length $2m$, so taking every other edge, $v_1v_2, v_3v_4, \dots, v_{2m-1}v_{2m}$, gives $m$ disjoint pairs of acquaintances covering everybody, that is a perfect matching.

blocks.body:
- Hall's condition must hold for every subset $S$. Checking only single vertices, or only $S = X$, is not enough: two students who both accept only project A satisfy $|N(\{x\})| \ge 1$ for each, but fail for the pair.
- A matching covering $X$ is perfect only when $|X| = |Y|$.
- Dirac's condition is sufficient, not necessary.
- In the Erdős–Gallai theorem the conclusion is a cycle of length at least $k$, not exactly $k$.

In matrix language, Hall's theorem implies that every doubly stochastic matrix is a weighted average (convex combination) of permutation matrices (the Birkhoff–von Neumann theorem; see [[matrices]]). Repeatedly removing perfect matchings from a regular bipartite graph shows that its edges can be coloured with $\Delta$ colours, an edge-colouring result of König that complements [[graph-coloring]]. In the language of [[set-systems]], a matching covering $X$ is a system of distinct representatives.

Hamiltonicity is the standard example of an NP-complete property, the subject of [[p-vs-np]]. The Erdős–Gallai theorem is an early result of [[extremal-graphs]], where one asks how many edges force a given structure.

1. Prove König's theorem for bipartite graphs from Hall's theorem: a maximum matching has the same size as a minimum vertex cover.
2. Show that a tree has at most one perfect matching.
3. Prove Ore's theorem by adapting the proof of Dirac's theorem.
4. Show that the bound in Dirac's theorem is also sharp for even $n$: for every even $n \ge 4$ find a non-Hamiltonian graph on $n$ vertices with minimum degree $n/2 - 1$.

sources.ref: Dirac, Some theorems on abstract graphs, Proc. London Math. Soc. (1952)
